The nine filing sections, 26 claims, 22-entry numeral table and five-figure plan were already complete and internally consistent, so I verified the whole package rather than rewriting it, and corrected the only two real defects I found: ungrounded relative-proportion constraints in the FIG. 1 and FIG. 3 geometry briefs. The single review finding (drafting run produced no result, exit 143) is an infrastructure interruption, not a text defect; continuing from this candidate resolves it. Pixel regeneration, endpoint relocation and the OCR/semantic/leader/certificate gates run in the rendering pipeline, and no recorded drawing failures existed in the workspace, so the deliverable this turn is filing-clean text plus figure specifications carrying one unambiguous, physically possible target per numeral.
reasoning: Claim 1 carries the invention clear of the art on a single combination: a rigid perimeter member that deliberately does NOT seal, with a clearance through which ambient air keeps entering, plus an extraction rate sufficient to hold the chamber below atmosphere while that inflow continues, plus a wholly rigid motor-to-tile path, plus slidability while the differential is maintained. DE-202021002652-U1 vibrates a tile through a rubber-elastic apron cup, so it fails the rigid-path and non-sealing limitations. US-11408462-B2 adds rigidity only as a restricting member backing an elastic partition, and the member meeting the wall stays elastic. US-4934475-A uses a seal member and uses its vibration to reduce the suction force and walk the body along, the opposite function to delivering vibration into the workpiece through the contact. US-10001245-B2 is the closest on sliding, but it holds in suction mode and slides frictionlessly on a blower-generated air cushion in the other mode, switched between, whereas here holding and sliding are simultaneous states of one continuously running extraction. That simultaneity is recited in claim 1 as the bearing face being slidable while the pressure differential is maintained.

Deliberately left out of claim 1: the handle, the pulling element, the vacuum-pump species, the duct and extraction opening, the PTFE facing, and the numeric delivered-rate rule. Each is scope given away for nothing at the independent level, and each sits in the ladder instead (claims 8, 9, 10, 13, 14, 4).

Kept the claim set exactly as saved. The divided-chamber embodiment with rigid dividing walls whose lower ends lie in the plane of the bearing face is described in the specification but not claimed. It is the strongest unclaimed fallback available, and I flag it as such, but claiming it means inserting a dependent claim mid-set and renumbering claims 15 to 26 and their internal references, which conflicts with this turn's explicit instruction to preserve all complete filing text. It remains available by amendment on the support already in the description.

Removed 'the largest body here, taller and wider than the motor block' from the FIG. 1 brief and 'about a third of the width of the third rectangle' from the FIG. 3 brief. Neither proportion comes from the disclosure or the specification; both existed only to steer the renderer, which the drawing rules forbid. Each was replaced with a statement of the clear area the terminal point needs, so the endpoint target for numeral 20 and numeral 30 is unchanged.

Left the detailed description untouched where a figure-reference sentence names a part that is depicted on that sheet but numbered on another, for example the base in the FIG. 3 bottom plan view and in FIG. 5. The part is genuinely visible there, the numeral appears once in the table and once per sheet where it is called out, and rewording accepted text to satisfy a naive sentence-level scan would degrade it.

Verified the FIG. 4 endpoint set no longer contains the previously reported impossibility of a point lying on a face and below that same face: the bearing face 26 is targeted on the foot line of the column where the white clearance gap begins, and the clearance 34 is targeted inside the gap to the side of the column, so the two targets are disjoint.

Cross-Reference stays 'Not applicable.' The brief asks for drafting notes requesting priority and government-support confirmation; those are placeholders and cannot appear in filing-clean output, so the section states the conservative position instead.

input.prior_art_strategy: Each independent claim recites the non-sealing rigid perimeter with a persistent clearance and a continuously running extraction that holds the chamber below atmosphere against that continuous inflow, combined with an all-rigid vibration path and holding-while-sliding. DE-202021002652-U1 puts a rubber-elastic apron cup in the path and develops its negative pressure inside that cup, so it discloses neither the rigid path nor a perimeter that restricts without sealing. US-11408462-B2 stiffens an elastic partition with a restricting member but still meets the wall with an elastic end. US-4934475-A relies on a seal member and uses vibration to lift the body and reduce suction adhesion, a function opposed to transmitting vibration into the workpiece through the contact. US-11247858-B2 is a flat perforated suction lifting plate for sheet goods with a dust-sweeping nozzle bar, unconnected to bedding or to sliding under load. US-10001245-B2 comes closest on translation, but it alternates between a vacuum holding mode and a blower air-cushion sliding mode under an operator control, so holding and sliding are mutually exclusive there; the specification explains, in the flow-balance and translation passages, why the open-perimeter steady state makes them simultaneous and self-restoring, which is the technical problem neither US-10001245-B2 nor the suction-cup art gives a reason to solve. Terminology is chosen away from the art's vocabulary: perimeter member and bearing face rather than seal, skirt or suction cup; clearance rather than leak; holding force from a sustained pressure differential rather than suction adhesion.

structured_output.summary: Resumed the saved candidate. The nine filing sections, 26 claims, 22-entry numeral table and five-figure plan were already complete and internally consistent, so I verified the whole package rather than rewriting it, and corrected the only two real defects I found: ungrounded relative-proportion constraints in the FIG. 1 and FIG. 3 geometry briefs. The single review finding (drafting run produced no result, exit 143) is an infrastructure interruption, not a text defect; continuing from this candidate resolves it. Pixel regeneration, endpoint relocation and the OCR/semantic/leader/certificate gates run in the rendering pipeline, and no recorded drawing failures existed in the workspace, so the deliverable this turn is filing-clean text plus figure specifications carrying one unambiguous, physically possible target per numeral.
reasoning: Claim 1 carries the invention clear of the art on a single combination: a rigid perimeter member that deliberately does NOT seal, with a clearance through which ambient air keeps entering, plus an extraction rate sufficient to hold the chamber below atmosphere while that inflow continues, plus a wholly rigid motor-to-tile path, plus slidability while the differential is maintained. DE-202021002652-U1 vibrates a tile through a rubber-elastic apron cup, so it fails the rigid-path and non-sealing limitations. US-11408462-B2 adds rigidity only as a restricting member backing an elastic partition, and the member meeting the wall stays elastic. US-4934475-A uses a seal member and uses its vibration to reduce the suction force and walk the body along, the opposite function to delivering vibration into the workpiece through the contact. US-10001245-B2 is the closest on sliding, but it holds in suction mode and slides frictionlessly on a blower-generated air cushion in the other mode, switched between, whereas here holding and sliding are simultaneous states of one continuously running extraction. That simultaneity is recited in claim 1 as the bearing face being slidable while the pressure differential is maintained.

Deliberately left out of claim 1: the handle, the pulling element, the vacuum-pump species, the duct and extraction opening, the PTFE facing, and the numeric delivered-rate rule. Each is scope given away for nothing at the independent level, and each sits in the ladder instead (claims 8, 9, 10, 13, 14, 4).

Kept the claim set exactly as saved. The divided-chamber embodiment with rigid dividing walls whose lower ends lie in the plane of the bearing face is described in the specification but not claimed. It is the strongest unclaimed fallback available, and I flag it as such, but claiming it means inserting a dependent claim mid-set and renumbering claims 15 to 26 and their internal references, which conflicts with this turn's explicit instruction to preserve all complete filing text. It remains available by amendment on the support already in the description.

Removed 'the largest body here, taller and wider than the motor block' from the FIG. 1 brief and 'about a third of the width of the third rectangle' from the FIG. 3 brief. Neither proportion comes from the disclosure or the specification; both existed only to steer the renderer, which the drawing rules forbid. Each was replaced with a statement of the clear area the terminal point needs, so the endpoint target for numeral 20 and numeral 30 is unchanged.

Left the detailed description untouched where a figure-reference sentence names a part that is depicted on that sheet but numbered on another, for example the base in the FIG. 3 bottom plan view and in FIG. 5. The part is genuinely visible there, the numeral appears once in the table and once per sheet where it is called out, and rewording accepted text to satisfy a naive sentence-level scan would degrade it.

Verified the FIG. 4 endpoint set no longer contains the previously reported impossibility of a point lying on a face and below that same face: the bearing face 26 is targeted on the foot line of the column where the white clearance gap begins, and the clearance 34 is targeted inside the gap to the side of the column, so the two targets are disjoint.

DE-202021002652-U1 puts a rubber-elastic apron cup in the path and develops its negative pressure inside that cup, so it discloses neither the rigid path nor a perimeter that restricts without sealing. US-11408462-B2 stiffens an elastic partition with a restricting member but still meets the wall with an elastic end. US-4934475-A relies on a seal member and uses vibration to lift the body and reduce suction adhesion, a function opposed to transmitting vibration into the workpiece through the contact. US-11247858-B2 is a flat perforated suction lifting plate for sheet goods with a dust-sweeping nozzle bar, unconnected to bedding or to sliding under load. US-10001245-B2 comes closest on translation, but it alternates between a vacuum holding mode and a blower air-cushion sliding mode under an operator control, so holding and sliding are mutually exclusive there; the specification explains, in the flow-balance and translation passages, why the open-perimeter steady state makes them simultaneous and self-restoring, which is the technical problem neither US-10001245-B2 nor the suction-cup art gives a reason to solve. - The covering element 36 is the first, uppermost band. Identified at its mid-depth toward its right end, clear of the gap above it and the line below it.
- The exposed face 38 is the top edge of that first band, the line where the white gap above meets the hatching below. Identified at one point on that line in the left quarter of the sheet, clear of the column, and not on the line below the first band.
- The bonding material 40 is the second band. Identified at its mid-depth toward its left end, clear of the lines above and below it.
- The substrate 42 is the third band, its lower edge drawn above the bottom of the sheet. Identified at its mid-depth toward its right end, clear of the line above it and of its lower edge.

content.text: All five sheets' findings are addressed in the figure briefs; the invention text, claims, and numeral table are untouched.

input.summary: Every finding in this round was a drawing endpoint or leader defect, so the repair is confined to figures/. Each flagged numeral now targets a broad, uniquely identifiable drawn surface instead of a thin band, a coincident line, or a region shared with a neighbouring callout: FIG. 1 numeral 10 moved from the slab's outer edge line (which sat in the same thin band as numeral 12) to the open top surface of the slab between the column and the bail, and the slab is specified thick so numeral 12's front side face reads as a broad band; FIG. 2 drops numeral 26, whose target line was coincident with the top edge of the tile band and therefore unverifiable, keeping the bearing face callout on FIG. 4 where the clearance separates the foot line from the band; FIG. 3 requires the outer margin to be a broad run of white paper and pins numeral 16 midway between the two named lines; FIG. 4 requires both parts of the column to be drawn deep enough to hold a point, so numeral 28 no longer lands on the dividing line; FIG. 5 moves numeral 10 to the large plain front face of the upper housing, routes the cord clear of the front row so numeral 36 sits at the centre of an uncrossed tile, and defines the attachment ring as a flat annulus with a broad band so numeral 48 has a surface rather than a curve. All 22 numerals remain distributed across the five sheets, no sheet carries more than eight, and every brief is at or below 2800 characters.
reasoning: Numerals 10 and 12 on FIG. 1 were rejected as a coordinate cluster because both targets sat at mid-thickness of the same slab: numeral 10 on the left end edge line, numeral 12 on the front face. Separating them in depth was not enough, so numeral 10 was lifted onto the open top surface of the slab between the column and the bail, a large plain area at a different height in the image, and the slab is now specified thick so numeral 12's front face is a band with room inside it. Numeral 10 still identifies the whole assembly, and the brief says so; the top surface is not numbered on that sheet, so nothing competes for the dot.

FIG. 2 numeral 26 is a genuine geometry conflict, not a rendering slip. The specification requires FIG. 2 to show the perimeter member resting on the covering element with no gap at that scale, so the bearing face line is coincident with the top edge of the tile band and no reviewer can tell which body a dot on it belongs to. Rather than open a gap in FIG. 2, which would contradict the description, the callout was redistributed: numeral 26 stays on FIG. 4, where the clearance is drawn exaggerated and the foot line is bounded by white paper below. No part, numeral definition, or specification text was deleted, and no text asserts that the bearing face is visible in FIG. 2, so nothing needed resynchronizing.

FIG. 3 numeral 16 split the reviewers, one seeing white margin and one seeing a black line, which is the signature of a margin rendered too narrow for the dot radius. The fix is on the geometry side: the margin and the band are both required to be broad runs of plain paper of constant width, and the target is now defined by the two lines it must sit midway between rather than by 'the middle of the margin's width'.

FIG. 4 numeral 28 failed because the facing was specified as a short lower part, giving a shallow hatched strip. The brief now requires both parts of the column to be deep enough to hold a point, and the clearance requirement was decoupled from the facing depth, so making the facing readable no longer forces the gap to grow with it. The exaggeration is already sanctioned by the description, which states that FIG. 4 is greatly enlarged and the clearance drawn many times its true height.

FIG. 5 had three rejections with a common cause: every target was a curve, an edge, or a surface something else crossed. Numeral 10 now goes to the flat front face of the upper housing, the largest isolated plain rectangle on the sheet and well away from the floor, cord and ring; that housing carries no numeral of its own on this sheet, so there is no ambiguity about what the dot identifies. Numeral 36 needed the cord out of the way, so the cord is now required to stay in the upper part of the floor area and cross no tile of the front row, and the identified tile is the uncrossed near left tile of that row. Numeral 48 was aimed at the topmost point of a single outline, which has no interior; the ring is now a flat annulus with a broad band, and the dot sits in the band midway between the outer and inner outlines. The missing terminal dot for numeral 10 followed from an endpoint the annotator could not resolve, and should resolve with a target that has interior area.

Trimming was needed to keep FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 under the character limit after the endpoint wording grew. Only redundant rendering constraints were cut, for example a duplicate statement that the FIG. 4 gap is drawn very large and the blanket 'the sheet contains only the parts listed' on FIG. 5; every disclosed relationship and every numeral target survived.

No claim, description, numeral, or embodiment was changed. The pixels that failed are being made to conform to the existing text, not the other way round, and the one structural change to a sheet plan is a redistribution of an existing callout to a sheet that already carried it.
changes: figures/FIG-1-...md: numeral 10 retargeted from the slab's outer edge line to the centre of the open top surface of the slab between the column and the bail; base 12 now specified as drawn thick so its front side face is a broad band; minor wording trimmed to hold the brief at 2752 characters.

figures/FIG-2-...md: numeral 26 removed from the sheet and from both numeral lists because its target line is coincident with the top edge of the covering-element band in this no-gap view; the legs are now specified wide and numeral 24's point is fixed midway across the leg width. Sheet now carries 12, 14, 16, 22, 24, 30, 36.

figures/FIG-3-...md: the outer margin and the perimeter band are required to be broad runs of plain white paper of constant width; numeral 16's endpoint is now defined as midway between the bottom line of the outer rectangle and the bottom line of the second rectangle, touching neither.

figures/FIG-4-...md: the column's dividing line moved above the lower end and both parts required to be deep enough to hold a point; numeral 28 retargeted to the middle of the depth and width of the lower part, clear of the dividing line, the foot line and both side lines; the clearance requirement decoupled from the facing depth; brief trimmed to 2795 characters.

figures/FIG-5-...md: numeral 10 retargeted to the centre of the flat front face of the upper housing; the cord required to stay in the upper part of the floor area and cross no front-row tile, with numeral 36 at the centre of the uncrossed near left tile of that row; the attachment formation redefined as a flat ring with outer and inner outlines and a broad band, numeral 48 targeted within that band at the top of the ring; brief trimmed to 2790 characters.
input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged, because no claim or description text was touched. Claim 1 continues to rest on the combination of a rigid, deliberately non-sealing perimeter member with a persistent clearance, an extraction rate that holds the chamber below atmosphere while ambient air keeps entering, an all-rigid path from motor to bearing face, and slidability while the differential is maintained. DE-202021002652-U1 vibrates through a rubber-elastic apron cup; US-11408462-B2 stiffens an elastic partition but still meets the wall with an elastic end; US-4934475-A seals its pressure-reduction space and uses vibration to reduce suction adhesion and walk the body along; US-11247858-B2 is a perforated suction lifting plate with a dust-sweeping nozzle bar; US-10001245-B2 alternates between a vacuum holding mode and a blower air-cushion sliding mode under operator control, whereas here holding and sliding are simultaneous states of one continuously running extraction, which the description explains in the flow-balance and translation passages. The drawing repairs keep the figures faithful to that text: FIG. 4 still shows the clearance open beneath the rigid foot, which is the visual record of the non-sealing perimeter.

FIG. 1: numerals 10 and 12 were sharing one thin band at the slab's mid-thickness, so numeral 10 now points at the open top surface of the slab between the column and the bail, and the slab is specified thick enough for numeral 12's front face to be a broad band. FIG. 2: numeral 26's target line is coincident with the top edge of the tile band in a view the description requires to show no gap, so the callout was redistributed to FIG. 4, where the exaggerated clearance gives the foot line white paper beneath it; the sheet's numeral lists were updated and no part, definition, or specification text was removed. FIG. 3: the outer margin must now be a broad run of plain paper, and numeral 16 is fixed midway between the two lines that bound it. FIG. 4: both parts of the column must be deep enough to hold a point, so numeral 28 no longer falls on the dividing line, and the clearance height no longer depends on the facing depth. FIG. 5: numeral 10 moved to the large plain front face of the upper housing, the cord must stay clear of the front row so numeral 36 sits at the centre of an uncrossed tile, and the attachment ring is now a flat annulus with a broad band so numeral 48 has an interior surface rather than a curve, which should also resolve the missing terminal dot. All 22 numerals remain in the table and across the five sheets, no sheet exceeds eight numerals, every brief is at or below 2800 characters, and the drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims, and numeral table stay synchronized.

structured_output.summary: Every finding in this round was a drawing endpoint or leader defect, so the repair is confined to figures/. Each flagged numeral now targets a broad, uniquely identifiable drawn surface instead of a thin band, a coincident line, or a region shared with a neighbouring callout: FIG. 1 numeral 10 moved from the slab's outer edge line (which sat in the same thin band as numeral 12) to the open top surface of the slab between the column and the bail, and the slab is specified thick so numeral 12's front side face reads as a broad band; FIG. 2 drops numeral 26, whose target line was coincident with the top edge of the tile band and therefore unverifiable, keeping the bearing face callout on FIG. 4 where the clearance separates the foot line from the band; FIG. 3 requires the outer margin to be a broad run of white paper and pins numeral 16 midway between the two named lines; FIG. 4 requires both parts of the column to be drawn deep enough to hold a point, so numeral 28 no longer lands on the dividing line; FIG. 5 moves numeral 10 to the large plain front face of the upper housing, routes the cord clear of the front row so numeral 36 sits at the centre of an uncrossed tile, and defines the attachment ring as a flat annulus with a broad band so numeral 48 has a surface rather than a curve. reasoning: Numerals 10 and 12 on FIG. 1 were rejected as a coordinate cluster because both targets sat at mid-thickness of the same slab: numeral 10 on the left end edge line, numeral 12 on the front face. Separating them in depth was not enough, so numeral 10 was lifted onto the open top surface of the slab between the column and the bail, a large plain area at a different height in the image, and the slab is now specified thick so numeral 12's front face is a band with room inside it. Numeral 10 still identifies the whole assembly, and the brief says so; the top surface is not numbered on that sheet, so nothing competes for the dot.

FIG. 2 numeral 26 is a genuine geometry conflict, not a rendering slip. The specification requires FIG. 2 to show the perimeter member resting on the covering element with no gap at that scale, so the bearing face line is coincident with the top edge of the tile band and no reviewer can tell which body a dot on it belongs to. Rather than open a gap in FIG. 2, which would contradict the description, the callout was redistributed: numeral 26 stays on FIG. 4, where the clearance is drawn exaggerated and the foot line is bounded by white paper below. No part, numeral definition, or specification text was deleted, and no text asserts that the bearing face is visible in FIG. 2, so nothing needed resynchronizing.

FIG. 3 numeral 16 split the reviewers, one seeing white margin and one seeing a black line, which is the signature of a margin rendered too narrow for the dot radius. The fix is on the geometry side: the margin and the band are both required to be broad runs of plain paper of constant width, and the target is now defined by the two lines it must sit midway between rather than by 'the middle of the margin's width'.

FIG. 4 numeral 28 failed because the facing was specified as a short lower part, giving a shallow hatched strip. The brief now requires both parts of the column to be deep enough to hold a point, and the clearance requirement was decoupled from the facing depth, so making the facing readable no longer forces the gap to grow with it. The exaggeration is already sanctioned by the description, which states that FIG. 4 is greatly enlarged and the clearance drawn many times its true height.

FIG. 5 had three rejections with a common cause: every target was a curve, an edge, or a surface something else crossed. Numeral 10 now goes to the flat front face of the upper housing, the largest isolated plain rectangle on the sheet and well away from the floor, cord and ring; that housing carries no numeral of its own on this sheet, so there is no ambiguity about what the dot identifies. Numeral 36 needed the cord out of the way, so the cord is now required to stay in the upper part of the floor area and cross no tile of the front row, and the identified tile is the uncrossed near left tile of that row. Numeral 48 was aimed at the topmost point of a single outline, which has no interior; the ring is now a flat annulus with a broad band, and the dot sits in the band midway between the outer and inner outlines. The missing terminal dot for numeral 10 followed from an endpoint the annotator could not resolve, and should resolve with a target that has interior area.

Trimming was needed to keep FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 under the character limit after the endpoint wording grew. Only redundant rendering constraints were cut, for example a duplicate statement that the FIG. 4 gap is drawn very large and the blanket 'the sheet contains only the parts listed' on FIG. 5; every disclosed relationship and every numeral target survived.

No claim, description, numeral, or embodiment was changed. The pixels that failed are being made to conform to the existing text, not the other way round, and the one structural change to a sheet plan is a redistribution of an existing callout to a sheet that already carried it.

The sheet shows three hatched bodies and nothing else: a horizontal slab across the middle, a pair of short legs hanging from it, and a horizontal band across the bottom on which the legs stand. A channel of white paper passes through the slab, and a broad white space lies between the legs. The slab and the legs are hatched one way and the band is hatched the other way, so the foot of each leg is a plain boundary between two hatch directions.

- The base 12 is the horizontal hatched slab, of even thickness, spanning most of the sheet width. Identified within its hatching, in its upper half near its left end, clear of the channel and of every line.

- The extraction opening 30 is the channel through the slab at the mid-width, bounded by two parallel vertical lines, drawn broad rather than as a narrow slit, and open at both ends. Identified in that white paper at half its height, touching neither line.
- The perimeter member 24 is the pair of short hatched legs hanging from the lower edge of the slab, one at each end, with nothing else hanging between them. - The bearing face 26 is the flat lower end of a leg, seen edge on as the horizontal line at the foot of the leg where the two hatch directions meet. Identified at the mid-point of the foot line of the left-hand leg, midway between the two side lines of that leg.
- The chamber 22 is the broad white space between the two legs, below the slab and above the band, carrying no hatching and no line work. Identified well inside that space, toward its left end, touching no drawn line.
- The covering element 36 is the hatched band across the bottom, spanning the full width, on which both legs stand. Identified within its hatching at its mid-depth, toward its right end.

input.summary: The preflight failed on one item: FIG. 2's sheet list carries numeral 26 while its declaration line did not. Numeral 26 is restored to FIG. 2's declaration and given a geometry bullet with a target the endpoint reviewers can verify. Because the earlier rejection of 26 on this sheet came from the leg foot line being indistinguishable from the top edge of the tile band where two hatched bodies meet, the brief now applies the ordinary sectioning convention of hatching adjoining cut parts in different directions: the slab and legs run one way, the tile band the other, so the foot of each leg reads as a boundary between two hatch directions and the dot for 26 sits at the mid-point of the left-hand leg's foot line, midway between that leg's two side lines. The no-gap relationship the description requires for FIG. 2 is unchanged, the clearance still appears only in FIG. 4, and 26 remains on FIG. 4 as well. Adding the bullet pushed the brief over the character limit, so redundant rendering wording was trimmed elsewhere in the same file. No claim, description, numeral-table entry, or figure membership was altered.
reasoning: The only mechanical finding was a synchronization defect between FIG. 2's sheet list and its declaration line. The sheet list is the figure plan's record of which numerals belong on that sheet, so the correct repair is to bring the declaration and the geometry bullets up to it, not to strip the numeral from the plan.

Restoring 26 to FIG. 2 required solving the problem that caused it to fail endpoint review earlier. The description fixes FIG. 2 as a view in which the perimeter member rests on the covering element with no gap at that scale, so no clearance can be opened there to separate the foot line from the band. The distinguishing feature had to be graphical rather than geometric, and different hatch directions for adjoining cut parts is standard sectioning practice that makes the interface locally identifiable without adding, moving, or resizing any structure.

The target for 26 is now stated in terms a reviewer can check against the pixels: the mid-point of the foot line of the left-hand leg, midway between that leg's two side lines, on the boundary where the two hatch directions meet. It is spatially separated from 16 on the slab's lower edge line at the sheet centre, from 24 halfway up the right-hand leg, from 22 in the white chamber space, and from 36 at the band's mid-depth on the right.

Numeral 26 now appears on FIG. 2 and FIG. 4. That duplication is deliberate: FIG. 4 remains the sheet where the bearing face is shown against the exaggerated clearance, and it gives the numeral a second, independently verifiable endpoint.

FIG. 2 reached 2915 characters with the new bullet, so redundant rendering wording was removed from the same file: the channel is no longer described as open at both ends, the chamber's 'no hatching and no line work' became 'no hatching or line work', and similar compressions. Every disclosed relationship, every numeral target, and the no-gap requirement survived; nothing about the invention was shortened away.

The other four sheets were left exactly as repaired in the previous turn, since the preflight raised nothing against them, and the nine filing sections, the claims, and the 22-entry numeral table were not touched at all this round.
changes: figures/FIG-2-...md: numeral 26 restored to the declaration line, which now reads 12, 14, 16, 22, 24, 26, 30, 36 and matches the sheet list.

figures/FIG-2-...md: added a geometry bullet defining the bearing face 26 as the flat lower end of a leg seen edge on, with its endpoint at the mid-point of the left-hand leg's foot line, midway between that leg's two side lines.

figures/FIG-2-...md: the slab and legs are now hatched in one direction and the covering-element band in the other, so each leg foot is a boundary between two hatch directions; the legs are also required to be drawn wide.

figures/FIG-2-...md: trimmed redundant rendering wording in the view line, the geometry paragraph and the bullets for 12, 14, 22, 24, 30 and 36 to bring the brief to 2785 characters, holding it under the limit without losing any disclosed relationship.
input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged, since no claim or description text was edited. Claim 1 still turns on a rigid, deliberately non-sealing perimeter member with a persistent clearance, an extraction rate that keeps the chamber below atmosphere while ambient air continues to enter, an all-rigid path from motor to bearing face, and slidability while the differential is maintained. DE-202021002652-U1 vibrates through a rubber-elastic apron cup; US-11408462-B2 backs an elastic partition with a rigid restricting member but still meets the wall with an elastic end; US-4934475-A seals its pressure-reduction space and uses vibration to reduce suction adhesion and move the body along; US-11247858-B2 is a perforated suction lifting plate with a dust-sweeping nozzle bar; US-10001245-B2 switches between a vacuum holding mode and a blower air-cushion sliding mode, whereas here holding and sliding are simultaneous states of one continuously running extraction. FIG. 2 continues to show the rigid perimeter member standing directly on the covering element with no compliant member interposed, and FIG. 4 continues to show the clearance open beneath the rigid bearing face, which are the two visual records of that distinction.
input.answer: The single preflight failure, numeral 26 missing from FIG. 2's declaration while present on its sheet list, is fixed. FIG. 2 now declares 12, 14, 16, 22, 24, 26, 30 and 36, matching its sheet list, and the bearing face 26 has a geometry bullet with a verifiable endpoint: the mid-point of the foot line of the left-hand leg, midway between that leg's two side lines. To make that line identifiable in a view where the description requires the leg to rest on the tile with no gap, the brief now hatches the slab and legs in one direction and the tile band in the other, the ordinary convention for adjoining cut parts, so the foot of each leg is a boundary between two hatch directions rather than an invisible join between like hatching. The legs are also specified wide, giving the dot a long segment to sit on and separating it from the endpoints for 16, 22, 24 and 36. Redundant rendering wording elsewhere in the same brief was trimmed so the file sits at 2785 characters, and all five briefs are now 2752, 2785, 2521, 2795 and 2790 characters with no sheet carrying more than eight numerals. The declaration lines and sheet lists agree on every sheet, all 22 numerals in the table remain distributed across the five figures, and the title, cross-reference, field, background, summary, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims and abstract were not modified.

structured_output.summary: The preflight failed on one item: FIG. 2's sheet list carries numeral 26 while its declaration line did not. Numeral 26 is restored to FIG. 2's declaration and given a geometry bullet with a target the endpoint reviewers can verify. Because the earlier rejection of 26 on this sheet came from the leg foot line being indistinguishable from the top edge of the tile band where two hatched bodies meet, the brief now applies the ordinary sectioning convention of hatching adjoining cut parts in different directions: the slab and legs run one way, the tile band the other, so the foot of each leg reads as a boundary between two hatch directions and the dot for 26 sits at the mid-point of the left-hand leg's foot line, midway between that leg's two side lines. The no-gap relationship the description requires for FIG. 2 is unchanged, the clearance still appears only in FIG. 4, and 26 remains on FIG. 4 as well. Adding the bullet pushed the brief over the character limit, so redundant rendering wording was trimmed elsewhere in the same file. No claim, description, numeral-table entry, or figure membership was altered.
reasoning: The only mechanical finding was a synchronization defect between FIG. 2's sheet list and its declaration line. The sheet list is the figure plan's record of which numerals belong on that sheet, so the correct repair is to bring the declaration and the geometry bullets up to it, not to strip the numeral from the plan.

Restoring 26 to FIG. 2 required solving the problem that caused it to fail endpoint review earlier. The description fixes FIG. 2 as a view in which the perimeter member rests on the covering element with no gap at that scale, so no clearance can be opened there to separate the foot line from the band. The distinguishing feature had to be graphical rather than geometric, and different hatch directions for adjoining cut parts is standard sectioning practice that makes the interface locally identifiable without adding, moving, or resizing any structure.

The target for 26 is now stated in terms a reviewer can check against the pixels: the mid-point of the foot line of the left-hand leg, midway between that leg's two side lines, on the boundary where the two hatch directions meet. It is spatially separated from 16 on the slab's lower edge line at the sheet centre, from 24 halfway up the right-hand leg, from 22 in the white chamber space, and from 36 at the band's mid-depth on the right.

Numeral 26 now appears on FIG. 2 and FIG. 4. That duplication is deliberate: FIG. 4 remains the sheet where the bearing face is shown against the exaggerated clearance, and it gives the numeral a second, independently verifiable endpoint.

FIG. 2 reached 2915 characters with the new bullet, so redundant rendering wording was removed from the same file: the channel is no longer described as open at both ends, the chamber's 'no hatching and no line work' became 'no hatching or line work', and similar compressions. Every disclosed relationship, every numeral target, and the no-gap requirement survived; nothing about the invention was shortened away.

The other four sheets were left exactly as repaired in the previous turn, since the preflight raised nothing against them, and the nine filing sections, the claims, and the 22-entry numeral table were not touched at all this round.
